title: Anatomy of a cartridge
summary: Hull, primer, powder, wad, shot and crimp: what is inside a clay cartridge, how each part affects the shot and which cartridges the rules of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting ban.

body.html: A cartridge holds everything for one shot: the hull with a metal head, the primer, powder, the wad and the shot. Shooters also say shell. 'Empties' are fired hulls.

The hull, or case, is a tube, most often plastic, with a metal head at the bottom. Paper hulls exist too, and some grounds prefer them because they leave less litter. A fired hull is usually 65–70 mm long, and it must suit the chamber of your gun (see Gauge and barrel length).

In the centre of the head sits the primer. When the firing pin strikes it, the primer gives a spark and ignites the powder. The powder does not explode but burns very fast, and the gases push the shot charge up the barrel.

Between the powder and the shot sits the wad. It works like a plug: it stops the hot gas blowing past the pellets, cushions the push and keeps the pellets together as they travel up the barrel. A plastic wad usually has a cup that protects the pellets and often gives a slightly tighter pattern.
A fibre or felt wad breaks down in nature, so many grounds insist on it. Biodegradable plastic wads also exist, but some grounds do not accept them.

Above the wad is the shot: several hundred small pellets. The top of the hull is closed by the crimp, most often a star of 6 or 8 folds. A good crimp holds everything firmly in place and helps each cartridge fire the same way as the last.

The FITASC rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting ban reloaded cartridges, that is, fired hulls filled again, for example at home. They also ban dispersers (inserts that spread the shot wider on purpose) and any other special device inside the cartridge. Mixed shot of different sizes or qualities, black powder and tracers (cartridges that leave a glowing trail) are banned too. So for competitions bring factory cartridges that comply with the rules.
The box usually shows the gauge, hull length, load, shot number or diameter, shot material and wad type, and often the velocity. Learn to read the box, and you will know what you are loading.

Some grounds add their own environmental rules for practice, for example fibre wads only or steel shot only: check the ground's rules before a trip. Empty cases go into the bin on the stand, and shooters with semi-automatics pick up their ejected cases when they leave.
Three numbers on the box have lessons of their own: the gauge (Gauge and barrel length), the shot size (Shot size) and the load (Load weight).

key_points.html: Cartridge = hull, primer, powder, wad, shot.
Plastic wad: often a slightly tighter pattern; fibre wad: breaks down in nature.
FITASC bans reloads, dispersers, mixed shot, black powder and tracers.
Read the box: gauge, length, load, shot, wad.
Empties go in the bin; semi-auto users pick up their cases.

did_you_know.html: After the shot a plastic wad flies on for several tens of metres beyond the stand. That is why the fields around old grounds can be full of wads, whereas fibre gradually breaks down.

quiz.q: What ignites the powder in a cartridge?
quiz.explain: The firing pin strikes the primer, which ignites the powder.

quiz.q: Why do many grounds require fibre wads?
quiz.explain: Fibre and felt break down, while ordinary plastic wads stay in the fields for years.

quiz.q: Which cartridges do the FITASC rules ban?
